claim: The mechanism of fork stalling at R-loops is distinct from that at protein-DNA barriers.

source: Since G4s on the lagging strand template are unlikely to be involved in leading strand restart (see below, Figure 4E), this data suggests that transcription induces G4s not only on the displaced non-template strand, but to some extent also on the template strand, which forms the leading strand template for the replisome at CD R-loops.
evidence: This is inferred from the transcription dependence of restart and the strand specificity of G4 effects.

evidence: This is inferred from the RNase H1 insensitivity of fork stalling at HO R-loops.

source: In contrast, since leading strand restart at HO R-loops is sensitive to RNase H1, G4s that block the leading strand polymerase, but not the CMG, appear to be stable only in ssDNA, that is, in the presence of the RNA:DNA hybrid on the opposite strand.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNase H1 sensitivity of restart at HO R-loops.

claim: The heterogeneity in the size and position of R-loops results in the formation of a sub-population of HO R-loops harboring G4s with fork blocking potential that are stable even after RNase H digestion of the RNA:DNA hybrid.
source: We hypothesize that the heterogeneity in the size and position of R-loops in our R-loop template (Figure 1) results in the formation of a sub-population of HO R-loops harboring G4s with fork blocking potential that are stable even after RNase H digestion of the RNA:DNA hybrid (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), while another sub-population of HO R-loops harbors G4s only with specific polymerase blocking potential that are resolved after RNase H digestion of the R-loop (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed heterogeneity of R-loops and the differential effects of RNase H1.

claim: Pif1 does not promote fork progression through CD R-loops, supporting the notion that its limited processivity is insufficient to resolve long RNA:DNA hybrids.
source: In contrast to RNase H1, we find that Pif1 does not promote fork progression through CD R-loops, supporting the notion that its limited processivity is insufficient to resolve long RNA:DNA hybrids (Figure 3C, lanes 1–3) (Pohl and Zakian, 2019).

source: However, RNase H1 and Pif1 together effectively eliminate fork stalling, uncoupling, and restart events CD R-loops (Figure 4C, lane 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

source: This suggests that RNase H1 and Pif1 coordinately promote fork progression at CD R-loops by eliminating both RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s from the leading strand template.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined effect of RNase H1 and Pif1 at CD R-loops.

claim: At HO R-loops Pif1 was markedly more efficient than RNase H1 in promoting fork progression.
source: Conversely, at HO R-loops Pif1 was markedly more efficient than RNase H1 in promoting fork progression (Figure 4C, lanes 5–7), which is consistent with the notion that G4s on the leading strand template cause fork stalling at HO R-loops.

claim: Addition of RNase H1 did not further promote fork progression at HO R-loops in the presence of Pif1.
source: Accordingly, addition of RNase H1 did not further promote fork progression at HO R-loops in the presence of Pif1 (Figure 4C, lane 8).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Fork stalling at R-loops can be induced by RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s on the leading strand template, while neither structure presents a fork block when formed on the lagging strand.
source: Together, the data suggests that fork stalling at R-loops can be induced by RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s on the leading strand template, while neither structure presents a fork block when formed on the lagging strand.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the RNase H1 and Pif1 experiments.

claim: On DNA templates that lack the Airn sequence, PDS does not impede DNA replication.
source: On DNA templates that lack the Airn sequence, PDS does not impede DNA replication (Figure 4D, lanes 1 + 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

source: In contrast, PDS induces a strong block to fork progression specifically at the Airn sequence in the HO orientation, that is, when the G-rich strand forms the leading strand template, even in the absence of R-loops (Figure 4D, lanes 3–6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: G4s forming on the G-rich strand of the Airn sequence in the absence of transcription impede replication forks only when stabilized by PDS.
source: Thus, G4s forming on the G-rich strand of the Airn sequence in the absence of transcription impede replication forks only when stabilized by PDS (Figure 4D, lanes 3 + 5), demonstrating that G4 stability determines the fork block potential of G4s.
evidence: This is inferred from the PDS dependence of fork stalling in the absence of R-loops.

claim: G4 stability determines the fork block potential of G4s.
source: Thus, G4s forming on the G-rich strand of the Airn sequence in the absence of transcription impede replication forks only when stabilized by PDS (Figure 4D, lanes 3 + 5), demonstrating that G4 stability determines the fork block potential of G4s.
evidence: This is inferred from the PDS experiments.

claim: Fork stalling is induced at HO R-loops even in the absence of PDS, and this effect is enhanced by PDS.
source: In contrast, fork stalling is induced at HO R-loops even in the absence of PDS, and this effect is enhanced by PDS (Figure 4D, lanes 7–10).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: R-loop formation modulates the G4 composition on the displaced strand.
source: Thus, R-loop formation modulates the G4 composition on the displaced strand, which is consistent with studies demonstrating a cooperative relationship between R-loops and G4s (De Magis et al., 2019; Duquette et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced fork stalling at HO R-loops compared to the Airn sequence alone, and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: R-loop formation induces the formation of fork-stalling G4s on the displaced strand but is not required for their maintenance.
source: Since RNase H1 is unable to prevent fork stalling at HO R-loops, R-loop formation induces the formation of fork-stalling G4s on the displaced strand but is not required for their maintenance.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNase H1 insensitivity of fork stalling at HO R-loops.

claim: In the CD orientation, PDS induces fork stalling at the Airn sequence in the absence of R-loops, but the extent of stalling is less pronounced than in the HO orientation.
source: In the CD orientation, PDS also induces fork stalling at the Airn sequence in the absence of R-loops, but the extent of stalling is less pronounced than in the HO orientation (Figure 4E, lanes 1–4; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the absence of R-loops, PDS induces leading strand restart at the Airn sequence, demonstrating that replisomes can pass some PDS-stabilized G4s and reprime leading strand synthesis downstream.
source: In addition, in the absence of R-loops, PDS induces leading strand restart at the Airn sequence, demonstrating that replisomes can pass some PDS-stabilized G4s and reprime leading strand synthesis downstream.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

source: Deletion of G4810-828 (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) eliminates the major PDS-induced fork block in the CD orientation, identifying this G4 as a fork block (Figure 4E, lanes 9–12).

claim: The deletion of G4810-828 exposes a novel downstream leading strand stall site that correlates with greatly increased leading strand restart in the presence of PDS.
source: The deletion of G4810-828 exposes a novel downstream leading strand stall site that correlates with greatly increased leading strand restart in the presence of PDS (Figure 4E, lanes 11 + 12).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

source: We conclude that G4s can induce fork stalling or uncoupling depending on G4 stability, which is consistent with the correlation of genetic instability with G4 stability in vivo (Piazza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PDS experiments and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Replisome uncoupling from leading strand synthesis at PDS-stabilized G4s indicates that some G4s pose a block to the leading strand polymerase, Pol ε, but not the CMG helicase.
source: Replisome uncoupling from leading strand synthesis at PDS-stabilized G4s indicates that some G4s pose a block to the leading strand polymerase, Pol ε, but not the CMG helicase (Figure 4E, native gel, lanes 2 + 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of uncoupling at G4s.

claim: While a fraction of uncoupling events at G4s leads to persistent unwinding in the absence of DNA synthesis, significant leading strand restart downstream of G4s is also observed.
source: Importantly, while a fraction of uncoupling events at G4s leads to persistent unwinding in the absence of DNA synthesis, we also observe significant leading strand restart downstream of G4s.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature.

source: This indicates that fork stalling at R-loops in the CD orientation is caused by RNA:DNA hybrids on the leading strand template.

evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

source: In summary, the data demonstrates that both RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s on the leading strand can induce fork stalling during R-loop-replisome collisions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the RNase H1 and PDS experiments.

claim: Both RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s have the potential to induce uncoupling of leading strand synthesis from fork progression.
source: Moreover, both RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s have the potential to induce uncoupling of leading strand synthesis from fork progression.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

source: Importantly, unwinding of the downstream oligonucleotide is not accompanied by the unwinding of the upstream DNA or RNA oligonucleotide (Figure 5B iii + iv).

claim: CMG can translocate on both DNA and RNA:DNA duplexes.
source: Thus, CMG can translocate on both DNA and RNA:DNA duplexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the helicase assay data.

claim: RNA:DNA hybrids on the leading strand at CD R-loops are not automatic blocks to fork progression.
source: Thus, RNA:DNA hybrids on the leading strand at CD R-loops are not automatic blocks to fork progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CMG helicase activity on RNA:DNA hybrids.

source: In the presence of a 5' flap, the RNA:DNA hybrid can be unwound by CMG, which may account for the generation of full-length replication products observed here in the presence of CD R-loops, and which could also explain the reduction in R-loop levels during CD transcription-replication collisions in human cells (Hamperl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the CMG helicase activity and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In the absence of a 5' flap, CMG can translocate on RNA:DNA hybrids without displacing the RNA.
source: In contrast, in the absence of a 5' flap, CMG can translocate on RNA:DNA hybrids without displacing the RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the CMG translocation data.

source: Since the RNA:DNA hybrid will form a block to Pol ε, which lacks strand-displacement activity, CMG translocation across RNA:DNA hybrids would induce uncoupling of leading strand synthesis from fork progression, thus providing a molecular basis for the RNase H1-sensitive uncoupling observed at CD R-loops (e.g. native gel, Figure 4C, lanes 1 + 2).

claim: The wildtype G4 sequence, but not its mutant derivative, strongly attenuates DNA unwinding by CMG when placed in the template strand.

evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CMG helicase assay data.

source: In the CD orientation and in the absence of R-loops, replication products obtained in the presence of Fen1/Cdc9 correspond primarily to full-length replication products, indicating that the G-rich strand of the Airn sequence does not pose an intrinsic obstacle to lagging strand synthesis (Figure 6A, lanes 1–4).

claim: In the presence of CD R-loops, leading strand stall and restart products are detected as before in the absence of Fen1/Cdc9.
source: In the presence of CD R-loops, leading strand stall and restart products are detected as before in the absence of Fen1/Cdc9 (Figure 6A, lanes 5 + 7).

source: This data is consistent with the notion that R-loop formation induces G4s on the displaced non-template strand, blocking the progression of the lagging strand polymerase during CD replisome collisions, thereby causing a gap in the nascent lagging strand.

evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and 7E.

source: The lagging strand gap is caused by G4810-828, as deletion of this G4 sequence is sufficient to eliminate the gap (Figure 7B, lanes 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

source: Consistent with RNA:DNA hybrids impeding lagging strand synthesis, HO R-loops cause an RNase H1-sensitive lagging strand gap also on templates in which G4810-828 has been deleted (Figure 7B, lanes 5–8).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Leading strand stalling persists at HO R-loops even in the presence of RNase H1 due to G4s on the G-rich leading strand template.
source: As shown above (Figure 4), leading strand stalling persists at HO R-loops even in the presence of RNase H1 due to G4s on the G-rich leading strand template, giving rise to stalled leading strand products that are similar in size to LagUS (Figure 7B, lane 8; Figure 7E iii).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and 7E.

claim: Pif1 promotes lagging strand synthesis at G4810-828 in the absence of R-loops.
source: Consistent with the observations above, we find that Pif1 promotes lagging strand synthesis at G4810-828 in the absence of R-loops (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The Pif1 function in promoting lagging strand synthesis at G4810-828 is specifically dependent on the Pif1 helicase activity.
source: This Pif1 function is specifically dependent on the Pif1 helicase activity, as mutation of the Pif1 Walker B motif, which has been shown to disrupt the helicase but not DNA binding activity of the human Pif1 orthologue (Dehghani-Tafti et al., 2019), abrogates the ability of Pif1 to promote lagging strand synthesis at G4810-828 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pif1 alone was unable to promote lagging strand synthesis at RNA:DNA hybrids.
source: In contrast, Pif1 alone was unable to promote lagging strand synthesis at RNA:DNA hybrids (Figure 7D, lanes 1 + 3) but promoted completion of lagging strand synthesis in conjunction with RNase H1 (Figure 7D, lanes 2 + 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Pif1 promoted completion of lagging strand synthesis in conjunction with RNase H1 at HO R-loops.
source: In contrast, Pif1 alone was unable to promote lagging strand synthesis at RNA:DNA hybrids (Figure 7D, lanes 1 + 3) but promoted completion of lagging strand synthesis in conjunction with RNase H1 (Figure 7D, lanes 2 + 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Both RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s can inhibit lagging strand synthesis at R-loops, and this inhibition is reversed by RNase H1 and Pif1, respectively.
source: We conclude that both RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s can inhibit lagging strand synthesis at R-loops, and this inhibition is reversed by RNase H1 and Pif1, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the lagging strand synthesis experiments.

claim: Studies in Escherichia coli have demonstrated that transcripts can prime leading strand synthesis after CD collisions of replisomes with RNAP.
source: Studies in Escherichia coli have demonstrated that transcripts can prime leading strand synthesis after CD collisions of replisomes with RNAP (Pomerantz and O'Donnell, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: T4 PNK treatment significantly increased the levels of leading strand restart products at CD R-loops.
source: Strikingly, T4 PNK treatment significantly increased the levels of leading strand restart products at CD R-loops (Figure 8A, lanes 1 + 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Unlike leading strand restart products obtained at CD R-loops in the absence of T4 PNK treatment, the novel restart products after T4 PNK treatment are sensitive to RNase H1 treatment.
source: Unlike leading strand restart products obtained at CD R-loops in the absence of T4 PNK treatment, these novel restart products are sensitive to RNase H1 treatment (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Formation of the T4 PNK-induced restart products is dependent on DNA synthesis at replisomes.
source: Moreover, formation of these products is dependent on DNA synthesis at replisomes (Figure 8B) and is not observed at HO R-loops, in which the RNA:DNA hybrid is on the lagging strand (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: The T4 PNK-induced restart products are not observed at HO R-loops, in which the RNA:DNA hybrid is on the lagging strand.
source: Moreover, formation of these products is dependent on DNA synthesis at replisomes (Figure 8B) and is not observed at HO R-loops, in which the RNA:DNA hybrid is on the lagging strand (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The data indicates the repriming of leading strand synthesis at the RNA 3'-OH of RNA:DNA hybrids.
source: Together, this data indicates the repriming of leading strand synthesis at the RNA 3'-OH of RNA:DNA hybrids (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is inferred from the T4 PNK experiments.

claim: Under the conditions used, Pol α, but not Pol δ or Pol ε, is capable of efficiently extending R-loop-associated RNA with DNA.
source: We find that under the conditions used here, Pol α, but not Pol δ or Pol ε, is capable of efficiently extending R-loop-associated RNA with DNA (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Extension by Pol α is limited to ~200–700 nt of DNA and is further increased to up to ~2.5 kb in the presence of all three polymerases, well below the length of complete restart products observed in the context of replisomes.
source: Extension by Pol α is limited to ~200–700 nt of DNA and is further increased to up to ~2.5 kb in the presence of all three polymerases, well below the length of complete restart products observed in the context of replisomes.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Leading strand restart at R-loop RNA during CD R-loop-replisome collisions is initiated by Pol α and extended by Pol δ and/or Pol ε.
source: This suggests that leading strand restart at R-loop RNA during CD R-loop-replisome collisions is initiated by Pol α and extended by Pol δ and/or Pol ε.
evidence: This is inferred from the polymerase extension data.

claim: While the formation of full-length leading strand products increases with the concentration of RNase H1 due to the resolution of the RNA:DNA hybrids, leading strand restart correlates inversely with the concentration of RNase H1.
source: While the formation of full-length leading strand products increases with the concentration of RNase H1 due to the resolution of the RNA:DNA hybrids, leading strand restart correlates inversely with the concentration of RNase H1 (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: RNase H1 treatment reduces the formation of uncoupled products in the native gel analysis.
source: Concomitantly, RNase H1 treatment reduces the formation of uncoupled products in the native gel analysis.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: A sub-saturating concentration of purified RNase H2 promotes leading strand restart specifically at CD R-loops.
source: Similarly, we find that a sub-saturating concentration of purified RNase H2 promotes leading strand restart specifically at CD R-loops (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RNase H generates a 3'-OH at the cleavage site, eliminating the requirement for T4 PNK to convert RNA 3'-P ends into 3'-OH ends for restart.
source: We note that RNase H generates a 3'-OH at the cleavage site (Hyjek et al., 2019), eliminating the requirement for T4 PNK to convert RNA 3'-P ends into 3'-OH ends for restart.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: R-loop-associated RNAs can prime leading strand restart when CMG can translocate over the RNA:DNA hybrid.
source: We conclude that R-loop-associated RNAs can prime leading strand restart when CMG can translocate over the RNA:DNA hybrid.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the T4 PNK and RNase H experiments.

claim: The specific structural configuration of R-loops determines the outcome of R-loop-replisome collisions, providing a mechanistic explanation for 'good' and 'bad' R-loops.
source: By reconstituting eukaryotic R-loop-replisome collisions in vitro, we demonstrate here that the specific structural configuration of R-loops determines the outcome of R-loop-replisome collisions, providing a mechanistic explanation for 'good' and 'bad' R-loops.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: 5' RNA flaps promote the unwinding of RNA:DNA hybrids by CMG on the leading strand.
source: 5' RNA flaps promote the unwinding of RNA:DNA hybrids by CMG on the leading strand.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CMG helicase assay data.

claim: The mechanism of 5' RNA flaps promoting unwinding of RNA:DNA hybrids is consistent with the observation that CD transcription-replication collisions reduce R-loop levels in cells.
source: This mechanism is consistent with the observation that CD transcription-replication collisions reduce R-loop levels in cells (Hamperl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In the HO orientation, forks may progress continuously, provided the displaced R-loop strand, which forms the leading strand template for the replisome, is devoid of inhibitory secondary DNA structure.
source: In the HO orientation, forks may also progress continuously, provided the displaced R-loop strand, which forms the leading strand template for the replisome, is devoid of inhibitory secondary DNA structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: G4s can inhibit DNA unwinding by CMG.
source: We demonstrate here that G4s can inhibit DNA unwinding by CMG, but it is conceivable that other DNA secondary structures forming on the displaced non-template strand similarly impede fork progression (Neil et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CMG helicase assay data.

claim: Other DNA secondary structures forming on the displaced non-template strand may similarly impede fork progression.
source: We demonstrate here that G4s can inhibit DNA unwinding by CMG, but it is conceivable that other DNA secondary structures forming on the displaced non-template strand similarly impede fork progression (Neil et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The ability of replisomes to pass through G4s is likely modulated by G4 stability.
source: The ability of replisomes to pass through G4s is likely modulated by G4 stability, which has been shown to influence the impact of G4s on genome stability (Piazza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the PDS experiments and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Forks can progress through R-loops harboring RNA:DNA hybrids or G4s with polymerase-stalling potential on the leading strand, resulting in the uncoupling of leading strand synthesis from replisome progression.
source: In addition, we demonstrate that forks can progress through R-loops harboring RNA:DNA hybrids or G4s with polymerase-stalling potential on the leading strand. This results in the uncoupling of leading strand synthesis from replisome progression.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Persistent uncoupling would be expected to induce the S phase checkpoint in cells, which may facilitate the clearance of polymerase blocks before S phase completion.
source: Persistent uncoupling would be expected to induce the S phase checkpoint in cells, which may facilitate the clearance of polymerase blocks before S phase completion (Pardo et al., 2017; Saldivar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Leading strand synthesis can be restarted at G4s by repriming downstream of the block, causing a gap in the nascent leading strand.
source: In the case of G4s, leading strand synthesis is reprimed downstream of the block, causing a gap in the nascent leading strand.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Transient uncoupling of leading strand synthesis from fork progression at G4s has been suggested to cause epigenetic instability in vertebrate cells, where repriming is promoted by PrimPol.
source: Transient uncoupling of leading strand synthesis from fork progression at G4s has been suggested to cause epigenetic instability in vertebrate cells, where repriming is promoted by PrimPol (Schiavone et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The leading strand restart observed at G4s appears to be significantly more efficient than that reported previously at DNA damage sites.
source: Notably, the leading strand restart observed at G4s here appears to be significantly more efficient than that reported previously at DNA damage sites (Taylor and Yeeles, 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature.

claim: Transient stalling of CMG may promote leading strand repriming at G4s.
source: We speculate that transient stalling of CMG, which may be less pronounced at DNA damage that does not pose a physical obstacle to the CMG, may promote leading strand repriming at G4s.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed efficiency of restart at G4s.

claim: Leading strand restart at RNA:DNA hybrids occurs by a mechanism in which Pol α extends the RNA 3' end with DNA before handover to the leading strand polymerase at the replisome.
source: Our data demonstrates that leading strand restart at RNA:DNA hybrids occurs by a mechanism in which Pol α extends the RNA 3' end with DNA before handover to the leading strand polymerase at the replisome (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the T4 PNK and polymerase extension experiments.

claim: The restart mechanism at RNA:DNA hybrids is analogous to that at DNA damage sites, where restart is initiated by TLS polymerases or Pol δ.
source: To a degree this restart mechanism is analogous to that at DNA damage sites, where restart is initiated by TLS polymerases or Pol δ (Guilliam and Yeeles, 2021; Guilliam and Yeeles, 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature.

claim: The involvement of Pol α in leading strand restart at RNA:DNA hybrids can be rationalized by its inherent preference for RNA/DNA junctions.
source: The involvement of Pol α can be rationalized by its inherent preference for RNA/DNA junctions (Perera et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The ability of transcripts to reprime leading strand synthesis was previously observed in E. coli.
source: The ability of transcripts to reprime leading strand synthesis was previously observed in E. coli (Pomerantz and O'Donnell, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: While the replicative DNA helicase in E. coli translocates on the lagging strand, eukaryotic replisomes are assembled around CMG on the leading strand, indicating that the respective mechanisms are fundamentally distinct.
source: However, while the replicative DNA helicase in E. coli translocates on the lagging strand, eukaryotic replisomes are assembled around CMG on the leading strand, indicating that the respective mechanisms are fundamentally distinct.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: CMG translocation across RNA:DNA duplexes allows the replisome to access RNA 3' ends of RNA:DNA duplexes.
source: We demonstrate that CMG can translocate across RNA:DNA duplexes, allowing the replisome to access RNA 3' ends of RNA:DNA duplexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CMG helicase assay data.

claim: The mechanism of leading strand restart at RNA:DNA hybrids requires the RNA 5' end of RNA:DNA hybrids to be annealed to the template strand in order to prevent unwinding by the replisome.
source: This mechanism requires the RNA 5' end of RNA:DNA hybrids to be annealed to the template strand in order to prevent unwinding by the replisome.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of CMG translocation.

claim: R-loop formation may be promoted by invasion of the DNA duplex by the RNA 5' end in order to limit topological clashes during the winding of the RNA around the template strand.
source: We note that R-loop formation may be promoted by invasion of the DNA duplex by the RNA 5' end in order to limit topological clashes during the winding of the RNA around the template strand (Belotserkovskii et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Flush RNA 5' ends may be encountered by the replisome at nicks in the RNA, analogous to lagging strand nicks.
source: Alternatively, flush RNA 5' ends may be encountered by the replisome at nicks in the RNA, analogous to lagging strand nicks (Vrtis et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Nicks in RNA may be generated by RNase H1 or RNase H2, whose activities are spatially and temporally limited, respectively.
source: Such nicks may be generated by RNase H1 or RNase H2, whose activities are spatially and temporally limited, respectively (Lockhart et al., 2019; Zimmer and Koshland, 2016).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Translocation of the CMG on dsDNA during replication termination or after encounter of lagging strand nicks induces ubiquitin-dependent replisome disassembly.
source: It is noteworthy that translocation of the CMG on dsDNA during replication termination or after encounter of lagging strand nicks induces ubiquitin-dependent replisome disassembly (Deegan et al., 2020; Vrtis et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CMG translocation on the RNA:DNA hybrid at CD R-loops may cause replisome disassembly, which would compete with fork restart and promote fork collapse instead.
source: It may, therefore, be interesting to test if CMG translocation on the RNA:DNA hybrid at CD R-loops can cause analogous replisome disassembly, which would compete with fork restart and promote fork collapse instead.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known properties of CMG translocation.

claim: The lagging strand template, which protects the CMG from ubiquitylation during normal fork progression, remains accessible at CD R-loops, contrary to the situation during termination or replisome encounter of lagging strand nicks, which may limit any potential replisome disassembly.
source: However, we also note that the lagging strand template, which protects the CMG from ubiquitylation during normal fork progression, remains accessible at CD R-loops, contrary to the situation during termination or replisome encounter of lagging strand nicks, which may limit any potential replisome disassembly.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural differences between CD R-loops and termination/lagging strand nicks.

claim: Both RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s can induce gaps in nascent lagging strands.
source: We find that both RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s can also induce gaps in nascent lagging strands.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Lagging strand G4s impede DNA replication in vivo.
source: This is consistent with lagging strand G4s impeding DNA replication in vivo and with G4s posing a block to Pol δ in primer extension assays (Dahan et al., 2018; Sparks et al., 2019b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: G4s pose a block to Pol δ in primer extension assays.
source: This is consistent with lagging strand G4s impeding DNA replication in vivo and with G4s posing a block to Pol δ in primer extension assays (Dahan et al., 2018; Sparks et al., 2019b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The block to lagging strand synthesis by RNA:DNA hybrids is surprising given the proficiency of the lagging strand machinery in removing RNA:DNA hybrids at Okazaki fragment 5' ends.
source: However, the block to lagging strand synthesis by RNA:DNA hybrids is surprising given the proficiency of the lagging strand machinery in removing RNA:DNA hybrids at Okazaki fragment 5' ends (Stodola and Burgers, 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature.

claim: Long RNA 5' flaps or G4s in the RNA strand may impinge on the ability of Pol δ and Fen1 to process RNA:DNA hybrids.
source: The reasons for this are currently unknown, but it is possible that long RNA 5' flaps or G4s in the RNA strand impinge on the ability of Pol δ and Fen1 to process RNA:DNA hybrids.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed block to lagging strand synthesis.

claim: RNA:DNA hybrid- and G4-induced blocks to fork progression, as well as leading and lagging strand synthesis, are mitigated by RNase H1 and Pif1, respectively.
source: We show that RNA:DNA hybrid- and G4-induced blocks to fork progression, as well as leading and lagging strand synthesis, are mitigated by RNase H1 and Pif1, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The data is consistent with in vivo studies demonstrating that both RNase H1 and Pif1 suppress genome instability at R-loops.
source: This data is consistent with in vivo studies demonstrating that both RNase H1 and Pif1 suppress genome instability at R-loops (Huertas and Aguilera, 2003; Li and Manley, 2005; Tran et al., 2017) and promote replication fork progression at R-loops and G4 sequences, respectively (Gan et al., 2011; Paeschke et al., 2011; Prado and Aguilera, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RNase H1 and Pif1 promote replication fork progression at R-loops and G4 sequences, respectively.
source: This data is consistent with in vivo studies demonstrating that both RNase H1 and Pif1 suppress genome instability at R-loops (Huertas and Aguilera, 2003; Li and Manley, 2005; Tran et al., 2017) and promote replication fork progression at R-loops and G4 sequences, respectively (Gan et al., 2011; Paeschke et al., 2011; Prado and Aguilera, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The coincidence of RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s at R-loops may limit the efficiency of RNase H1 overexpression to resolve R-loops.
source: We note that the coincidence of RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s at R-loops may limit the efficiency of RNase H1 overexpression to resolve R-loops, which is commonly used to assess the contribution of R-loops to TRC.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for both RNase H1 and Pif1 to fully resolve R-loop-induced replication defects.

claim: R-loops in both the CD and HO orientation can induce persistent fork stalling, which requires the RNA:DNA hybrid- and/or G4-resolving activities of RNase H1 and Pif1 for continued fork progression.
source: R-loops in both the CD and HO orientation can induce persistent fork stalling, which requires the RNA:DNA hybrid- and/or G4-resolving activities of RNase H1 and Pif1 for continued fork progression.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Replisomes have an intrinsic capacity to progress through R-loops by bypassing or unwinding G4s or RNA:DNA hybrids.
source: However, we also find that replisomes have an intrinsic capacity to progress through R-loops by bypassing or unwinding G4s or RNA:DNA hybrids.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Despite the potential to induce nascent strand gaps, continued fork progression may be beneficial in order to establish homology-directed repair-competent chromatin on sister chromatids.
source: Despite the potential to induce nascent strand gaps, continued fork progression may be beneficial in order to establish homology-directed repair-competent chromatin on sister chromatids (Nakamura et al., 2019; Saredi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nascent strand discontinuities at R-loops may be processed post-replicatively, which could allow the timely progression of S phase.
source: Nascent strand discontinuities at R-loops may also be processed post-replicatively (Wu et al., 2020), which could allow the timely progression of S phase.
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Replisome bypass of R-loops may promote the resolution of R-loops analogous to the repair of DNA-protein crosslinks.
source: Alternatively, replisome bypass of R-loops may promote the resolution of R-loops analogous to the repair of DNA-protein crosslinks (Sparks et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The molecular characterization of R-loop-replisome collision enhances our understanding of the mechanism(s) by which G4 ligands can affect the growth of cancer cells.
source: The molecular characterization of R-loop-replisome collision presented here enhances our understanding of the mechanism(s) by which G4 ligands can affect the growth of cancer cells (De Magis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The system developed here will aid future studies directed at characterizing the molecular functions of the multitude of additional factors implicated in the processing of RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s.
source: Moving forward, we expect that the system developed here will aid future studies directed at characterizing the molecular functions of the multitude of additional factors implicated in the processing of RNA:DNA hybrids and G4s (Garcia-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; Lerner and Sale, 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about future applications of the system.

claim: Many additional factors, such as RNAP, transcription factors, and specialized chromatin structures, are associated with R-loops in vivo and further influence the outcome of R-loop-replisome collisions.
source: While the experiments reported here were designed to specifically assess the impact of the R-loop nucleic acid structure on replisome progression, many additional factors, such as RNAP, transcription factors, and specialized chromatin structures, are associated with R-loops in vivo and further influence the outcome of R-loop-replisome collisions (Castellano-Pozo et al., 2013; Garcia-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; Garcia-Pichardo et al., 2017; Garcia-Rubio et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

source: Reconstitution of R-loop-replisome collisions on chromatin templates will thus be an interesting challenge for future studies.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

source: Moreover, since DNA supercoiling affects R-loop formation and stability (Chedin and Benham, 2020), it will be of interest to investigate the impact of R-loops on replication fork progression in topologically closed DNA templates.
